info.text: Four questions on Primer 1: the assignment arrow, functions and named arguments, vectors, comparisons and type coercion. Unlimited attempts, immediate feedback, zero weight.

questiontext.text:
Five students sat an OSCE station and scored 78, 70, 91, 55 and 83.

osce <- c(78, 70, 91, 55, 83)

sum(osce >= 70)

What does the second line print?

generalfeedback.text: 4. The comparison gives one TRUE or FALSE per student, and sum() counts each TRUE as 1. The bar matters: >= keeps the student who scored exactly 70, > drops them. Whenever a threshold is "70 or above", "at least 40" or "under 5", that single character decides whether a real person is counted.

feedback.text: That is the answer to sum(osce > 70), which drops the student who scored exactly 70. >= means "greater than or equal to", so that student is counted and the answer is 4.
That is how many students there are, which is length(osce). Only four of them reached 70; the student who scored 55 did not.
That is the total of the five marks — sum(osce). Here sum() is being given the comparison, not the marks, so it adds up TRUEs rather than scores.

questiontext.text:
You combine three values and R prints this:

c(1, 2, "three")
#> [1] "1"     "2"     "three"

Those quotation marks around 1 and 2 matter. What can you no longer do?

generalfeedback.text: A vector holds one type only. Mix them and everything is silently converted to the most permissive type — text — so the numbers stop behaving like numbers. In real data this happens when one cell in a column holds "NA", "-", "<1" or a stray space, and it is why glimpse() showing <chr> where you expected <dbl> is worth a second look.

answer.text: Anything arithmetic — all three values are now text, so mean() will not work

feedback.text: Correct. One piece of text converted the whole vector.

answer.text: Nothing — R remembers which two were numbers

feedback.text: It does not. There is no mixed state: the vector is entirely text now, and "1" is a character that happens to look like a number.

answer.text: You can still average the first two, just not the third

feedback.text: No. A vector is all one type by definition, so there are no longer any numbers in it to average. You would have to convert with as.numeric() first, and then decide what to do about "three".

answer.text: You can no longer print it — R errors on mixed types

feedback.text: The opposite of the problem. R never errors here; it converts quietly and prints something that looks nearly right, which is exactly why this catches people out.

questiontext.text:
scores holds five marks. What does this line give you?

scores > 70

generalfeedback.text: Five TRUE/FALSE values — one per element. R applies the comparison to the whole vector at once, which is why you never need a loop to ask a question of every row. That vector is what sum() counts and what filter() uses to decide which rows to keep.

answer.text: A vector of five TRUE/FALSE values, one per mark

feedback.text: Correct — and that is the building block of everything you will do with filter() on Day 1.

answer.text: A single TRUE or FALSE for the vector as a whole

feedback.text: No. The comparison is applied element by element, so you get one answer per mark. Collapsing five answers into one takes a further step — any(), all() or sum().
Not by itself, though you are one step away: scores[scores > 70] uses those TRUEs and FALSEs to pull out the values. The comparison alone returns the TRUEs and FALSEs, not the marks.
That is sum(scores > 70). The comparison produces the TRUEs and FALSEs; sum() is what turns them into a count.

generalfeedback.text: 3.14. A function takes its arguments in brackets, separated by commas, and naming them — digits = 2 rather than just 2 — makes the line readable to somebody who does not remember the argument order. Prefer named arguments; your reader, including future you, will not have the help page open.

feedback.text: That is digits = 3. The argument counts decimal places, not significant figures — for significant figures you want signif().
That is round(3.14159), with no digits at all — the default is zero decimal places.
No — digits = 2 is an instruction about how to round, not the value returned. The function still hands back a rounded version of 3.14159.
